claims.text: Tempered martensitic steels exhibit conventional temper embrittlement.
Temper embrittlement in martensitic steels occurs through impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
The narrow temperature range of temper embrittlement can be exploited to produce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The proposed initial material is untempered martensitic steel with a relatively uniform microstructure and minimal grain-boundary segregation.
Tempering within the embrittlement range activates segregation of impurity atoms such as phosphorus and sulfur to grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary precipitates and segregated impurity species reduce grain-boundary cohesive strength.
At intermediate tempering temperatures, grain-boundary impurity segregation decreases cohesion and causes brittle behavior.
At lower tempering temperatures, insufficient impurity segregation preserves a more ductile response.
At higher tempering temperatures, dissolution or reprecipitation of impurities restores a more ductile response.
The treated steel will be ductile initially, become brittle within a narrow tempering-temperature window, and return to ductile behavior outside that window.
Untempered martensitic steel has high hardness and lacks significant temper embrittlement.
The proposed behavior is limited to conventional alloys susceptible to impurity-segregation-driven temper embrittlement.
The proposed ductile–brittle–ductile behavior is not expected in compositionally complex or high-entropy alloy systems.
